assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's strontium clock work, moved timekeeping and frequency metrology to the 10^-18 level. Few advances so directly embody the idea that knowledge is limited by what can be measured and how accurately. The impact runs from redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy and fundamental-constant tests to searches for dark matter and variation of constants.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and realised the first lattice clock; Ye led the demonstration of record systematic uncertainty and stability. Both are in the supplied credit and form a clean two-person prize. Others in the field (for example ion-clock and Hall-Hansch comb groups) are outside the credited names and the earlier 2005 prize already covered combs.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs have reproduced 10^-18-class performance, the interpretation is stable and recognition is timely. Redefinition of the SI second is still pending, though that does not undermine the physical achievement.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for ion control.
I recall but have not verified the exact sequence of record uncertainty claims between groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and the founding of quantum cryptography turned quantum measurement limits into a practical information-security principle. It is conceptually original, linked to the foundations recognised in 2022, and has led to commercial and national-scale deployments and a large experimental field in which optical quantum states are manipulated at the single-photon level.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are the authors of the 1984 protocol and the clear core of the credit. Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol is a separate, independent contribution; the supplied credited names list him twice with two spellings ('Artur Ekert' and 'Artur K. Ekert'), which I would treat as one person and which I do not use here to avoid ambiguity. Whether Ekert should share is a genuine allocation question.
assessment.maturity: Four decades of experimental confirmation, from the first bench demonstration to field networks, make this mature and arguably overdue, with the 2022 prize having already honoured the related entanglement tests.
uncertainties: Ekert versus Bennett-Brassard allocation is unresolved and the duplicated name entry should be cleaned up.
Security of real implementations (side channels) is still an engineering concern, though not a challenge to the principle.
Possible perception that 2022 partially covered this area.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices provide a controllable platform for emulating Hubbard-type many-body physics, including the Mott insulator transition, Fermi-Hubbard antiferromagnetism and quantum gas microscopy. The idea of programmable analogue quantum simulation is original and has strongly changed both atomic physics and condensed matter research.
assessment.attribution: The credited list has five names. Zoller and Cirac with Jaksch supplied the theoretical proposal; Greiner, Bloch and Esslinger delivered the key experiments (Mott insulator, Fermi-Hubbard, microscopy). A three-person prize of Bloch, Esslinger and Zoller is a reasonable but imperfect compromise, leaving Greiner and Cirac out. Credit for the microscope and the Mott transition between Greiner and Bloch is a known sensitivity.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups and platforms over two decades. Open questions concern what quantum simulation has yet established beyond classical computation, but the experimental achievements stand independently.
uncertainties: Selection from five credited names forces the omission of Greiner and Cirac.
Overlap in credit with trapped-ion (B011) and Rydberg (B037) proposals involving Zoller and Cirac.
I recall details of early Mott-transition priority only from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres created a room-temperature solid-state qubit and sensor of magnetic fields, electric fields, temperature and strain at the nanoscale. Optically addressed single defects, coherence in the solid state and spin-selective readout resonate with my own work in rare-earth-ion crystals and quantum sensing, and the applications range from biology to condensed-matter probes.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko reported the first optical detection and coherent control of a single NV centre in 1997 and 2004 respectively; Lukin contributed nanoscale sensing, quantum registers and many-body NV experiments. A three-person prize from the supplied names is fair, though Awschalom, Hanson and others are outside this entry and arguably equally decisive for the broader field (B008 covers related work).
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent groups, with active commercial development. Sensing applications are still maturing, while the foundational discovery is well established.
uncertainties: Overlap with the related B008 entry on optical interfaces to spins, where Wrachtrup also appears.
Allocation between early discovery and later applications is not clear from the supplied text.
I have not independently verified the precise dates of first-observation claims.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller trapped-ion quantum gate proposal and its realisation, along with Blatt's work on entanglement and algorithms, established ions as the most precise quantum processors with the highest gate fidelities. The Nobel committee has already honoured Wineland for ion control, so the case rests on quantum computing and simulation as a distinct advance.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the clear theoretical originators of the ion-gate scheme; Blatt is a leading experimentalist, though Wineland's group demonstrated the first gate and Monroe and others are not in the credited list. The overlap with the Cirac-Zoller credit in B016 makes joint decisions on the two entries delicate.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of experiments confirm the approach and commercial ion computers exist. Scaling remains an open question, which affects how soon it would be timely.
uncertainties: The 2012 prize for Wineland partly overlaps in experimental technique.
Credit for the first experimental gate is not in the supplied names.
Scaling to useful quantum advantage remains unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry combines laser cooling, coherent beam splitting and phase readout to give extraordinary sensitivity to gravity, rotation and fundamental constants, and is used for tests of the equivalence principle and for gravimetry. It is a direct, high-precision measurement method with a clear conceptual identity.
assessment.attribution: Four names are credited; Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich each made decisive early contributions (theory of the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, first atom interferometers and precision inertial and gravity measurements). Schmiedmayer's matter-wave interferometry on chips is a distinct strand. Choosing three leaves out Schmiedmayer and Chu-style contributions, which are not in the list.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups and in use, but the largest-scale applications (space-based and long-baseline fundamental tests) are still to come. The field is mature in methods but not yet in headline discoveries.
uncertainties: Competing claims for early realisation among several groups, including those outside the supplied names.
Overlap with the earlier laser-cooling and Ramsey-method prizes.
Impact is as yet mostly in metrology rather than a decisive discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Strongly interacting Fermi gases and the BEC-BCS crossover, explored through Feshbach-resonance tuning, give a clean laboratory realisation of fermionic superfluidity, unitarity and universal thermodynamics, with relevance to neutron matter and high-temperature superconductors. It is a natural extension of the cold atom Nobel prizes of 1997 and 2001.
assessment.attribution: Grimm, Salomon, Thomas, and also Jin, Ketterle and Zwierlein contributed to condensation of molecules and the crossover; Jin's death in 2015 complicates credit. Among the supplied names, the three give a reasonable but not complete grouping; Ketterle's group and Zwierlein are not listed.
assessment.maturity: Replicated by several groups and mature experimentally, with theoretical interpretation well controlled. The subfield has settled into precision studies.
uncertainties: Important contributors such as Deborah Jin (deceased) are outside the credited names.
Whether the physics is considered a refinement of the 2001 BEC prize.
Priority for the first molecular BEC and the crossover observation is complicated among groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The titanium-sapphire laser together with Kerr-lens and semiconductor saturable-absorber mode-locking made femtosecond pulses practical across laboratories, enabling spectroscopy, frequency combs, attosecond science and biomedical imaging. As a laser spectroscopist I regard it as foundational instrumentation, though the Nobel track record favours the uses (2018 chirped pulse amplification, 2023 attosecond) over earlier enabling tools.
assessment.attribution: Moulton invented the Ti:sapphire gain medium; Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking; Keller developed SESAM mode-locking. These three roles are distinct yet complementary and the supplied names support a three-person prize. Other contributors to Kerr-lens work (Spence, Kean) are not in the list.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature and ubiquitous, so recognition is not premature; the question is whether it counts as an invention of sufficient fundamental weight relative to the many existing laser prizes.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier laser, comb and ultrafast prizes.
Credit for Kerr-lens mode locking is shared with people outside the supplied names.
Whether the committee views this as invention versus discovery in scope.
